title: Strategic Misrepresentation
hook: A promise can be built to win approval, not to survive contact with the work.
counterintuition: A low budget or bold promise may be a strategy, not a mistake; expose the incentive, then require assumptions that survive after approval.
tryThisNow: Find one plan that needs a yes. Write who benefits if the estimate is too rosy, then add one outside check before the yes.
keyTakeaway: Strategic misrepresentation happens when a promise is shaped to get approval. Test incentives and assumptions before the project starts.

breakdown.fastRead: The weather log beside the hotel dashboard shows three storm nights missing from the lobby budget. Miranda wants a yes, so the timeline looks smooth. That is strategic misrepresentation. She marks the log, adds storm-delay assumptions to the budget page, and makes the owner approve the real range before signing. The buyer can see the range before the vote.
breakdown.deepRead:
Miranda may miss a storm delay because she hopes the work goes well. Strategic misrepresentation is different. The person making the promise knows the number, schedule, or benefit case is bent, but the bend helps the project get a yes.

Before approval, a low budget sounds disciplined. A short timeline sounds capable. A large benefit claim sounds ambitious. After approval, the missing costs and delays become everyone's problem. The person who shaded the estimate may already have won the prize: funding, status, permission, or momentum.

The promise is part of the strategy.

You correct it by inspecting incentives before believing the promise. Who gets rewarded if this is approved? Who pays if the estimate is wrong? Which assumptions would look different if the same person had to manage the overrun? Then add a visible check: outside reference cases, signed assumptions, staged funding, independent cost review, or a post-approval owner for each claim.

A bold promise can be honest and worth backing. Do not treat a proposal as neutral when the proposer benefits from making it look easier, cheaper, faster, or more popular than it is.
breakdown.fullRead:
The score sheet in the climate NGO image test shows that the more dramatic campaign promise wins donors faster. Philippe, the campaign director, likes the result. The image test says supporters will click if the page promises a large policy win this year. The policy team knows the win is possible but unlikely. He has to decide whether the promise is a forecast or bait for approval.

Strategic misrepresentation lives in that gap. It is not simple error. It is not ordinary optimism. It is a shaped claim, built for a decision moment. A budget is trimmed because a full budget would be rejected. A schedule is compressed because a real schedule would miss the funding window. A benefit is inflated because a modest benefit would not clear the board.

What would this plan say if approval were already guaranteed?

Bent Flyvbjerg's work on megaprojects and risk made the pattern blunt: large projects often reach approval through claims that understate cost or overstate benefit. Jones and Euske's Strategic Misrepresentation in Budgeting points to the same problem inside budgeting systems. The issue is structural. If the prize goes to the proposal that looks best before work starts, people learn to polish the promise and bury the risk.

That does not mean every proposer is corrupt. Incentives can bend honest people by degrees. An admissions team may widen an applicant-pool forecast because the larger number helps a program survive. A shipping department may soften claim rates because the budget review is brutal. A hotel manager may omit weather delays because the owner wants a clean renovation story.

A good approval process distrusts the incentive, not just the person.

An art fair sales readout shows the smaller version. Roxanne presents early buyer interest as if it were firm approval for a bigger booth next year. The consent form on the table tells a different story: half the buyers allowed follow-up but did not commit. If the fair uses the inflated approval story, the booth grows before demand is real. If Roxanne marks the approval risk and separates interest from commitment, the next choice is harder but cleaner.

The practical correction has four parts. First, list the claims that made the proposal attractive. Second, ask who benefits from each claim being high or low. Third, compare the claim with outside cases, not only internal confidence. Fourth, attach an owner to the assumption after approval, so the promise cannot disappear once funding is won.

The limit is that no plan can remove uncertainty. New work requires estimates. A hard standard should not punish every team that misses a forecast honestly. The key distinction is incentive-aware evidence. Was the assumption visible? Was there an outside check? Did the proposer gain by hiding the weak part? Did the approval process reward candor or only the prettiest number?

Before the choice moves forward, make the promise carry its future cost. Put the incentive beside the estimate. Put the outside case beside the forecast. Put the owner beside the assumption. A plan that still deserves approval after that deserves a real yes.

examples.title: Miranda restores the storm nights
examples.scenario: A weather log sits beside the hotel guest-review dashboard in Brighton at 10:20 a.m. Miranda must decide whether to send a lobby renovation estimate that leaves out three storm-delay nights. She writes strategic misrepresentation on the log, adds the delay range to the budget page, and changes the owner packet before the general manager signs.
examples.whatToDo: Put the weather-delay range into the approval packet before the renovation estimate goes forward.
examples.whyItMatters: The clean timeline helps win approval, but the hotel will still live with storm delays after the work starts.

planSpec.domain: a hotel guest-review dashboard applying Strategic Misrepresentation under operational pressure

examples.title: Philippe tempers the donor promise
examples.scenario: "This image wins if we promise a policy shift by December," the analyst says during a climate NGO image test in Paris. Philippe must decide whether to use the score sheet without the policy team's probability range. He circles promise on the sheet, adds the range beside the winning image, and changes the campaign copy while the fundraising lead watches.
examples.whatToDo: Pair the winning image with the policy probability range before using the promise in donor copy.
examples.whyItMatters: The promise gets clicks, but approval from donors should not rest on a result the policy team would not stand behind.

examples.title: Roxanne separates interest from approval
examples.scenario: The consent form smells of fresh ink in the art fair sales readout room in Basel. Roxanne must decide whether to report buyer interest as approval for a larger booth. She marks approval on the form, separates follow-up consent from signed purchase intent, and changes the readout in front of the gallery director.
examples.whatToDo: Report follow-up consent and purchase intent as separate numbers before asking for a larger booth.
examples.whyItMatters: Interest can be made to look like demand when a bigger booth needs approval. The fair needs the real commitment level.

planSpec.domain: a art fair sales readout applying Strategic Misrepresentation under operational pressure

examples.title: Bjorn refuses the softened claim rate
examples.scenario: You are holding a shipment seal in a Rotterdam claims office while the quarterly budget run is due by 5 p.m. Bjorn must decide whether to exclude two damaged pallets from the claim rate because the shipping team needs a lower budget number. He writes budget on the seal, restores the pallets to the run, and changes the file in front of finance.
examples.whatToDo: Restore the damaged pallets to the claim rate before using the number in the budget run.
examples.whyItMatters: The lower claim rate helps the budget pass, but it shifts real damage costs into the next quarter.

planSpec.domain: a shipping claim run applying Strategic Misrepresentation under operational pressure

examples.title: Celeste tests the applicant forecast
examples.scenario: It took Celeste one admissions cycle in Seattle to see that the applicant-pool review always grew right before funding votes. At 6:05 p.m. in the enrollment office, Celeste, the program analyst, studies a parking ticket from the open-house overflow lot and predicts the dean will fund another recruiter. Before the vote, she must decide whether the incentive is shaping the forecast or whether outside applications support it.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the forecast with outside application trends before using the overflow lot as proof of demand.
examples.whyItMatters: The packed lot helps the program story, but the incentive to win a recruiter can inflate the applicant pool.

planSpec.domain: a admissions applicant-pool review applying Strategic Misrepresentation under operational pressure

examples.title: Dario's rugby form postmortem
examples.scenario: What won the funding: better form or a better-looking injury forecast? Dario asks that after a rugby form debate in Cardiff reviews a safety glove from the pilot session. The coach had trimmed expected injury rates to get approval for the training block. Dario marks strategic on the glove and changes the next proposal so injury assumptions require an outside season comparison.
examples.whatToDo: Attach an outside season comparison to injury assumptions before approving the next training block.
examples.whyItMatters: The safer-looking forecast helped the block start. The team needs assumptions that survive after approval.

reviewCards.front: A proposal looks too clean right before approval. What outside estimate should test the proposal?
reviewCards.back: Use an outside-view estimate, incentives check, and downside review. A clean proposal may be optimized for approval.
Ask who benefits if the estimate is rosy and who pays if it is wrong.
Visible assumptions, outside reference cases, staged funding, and an owner after approval.

reviewCards.front: How is this different from optimism?
reviewCards.back: Optimism may be sincere error; strategic misrepresentation bends the claim because the bend helps win approval.

reviewCards.front: A benefit claim wins clicks. What should happen before it is used?
reviewCards.back: Pair it with the probability range or outside evidence that must survive after approval.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Expose the incentive behind the promise, then require outside checks and owned assumptions before approval.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a number looks clean before approval, then I will ask who benefits from that cleanliness.
If a claim wins attention, then I will pair it with a probability range before using it.
If internal confidence is high, then I will compare the estimate with outside cases before approving.
If assumptions unlock funding, then I will assign owners who live with those assumptions after approval.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one proposal seeking a yes. Add a line naming who benefits from the estimate and one outside case that checks it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review an approved plan and compare its original assumptions with what the owners now face.

memorableLines.text: The promise is part of the strategy.
A good approval process distrusts the incentive, not just the person.
A plan that still deserves approval after that deserves a real yes.
